module_title: Waterfall Mechanism, Commercial Wisdom, and Avoidance Transactions
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams, corporate litigators, and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the absolute boundaries of the IBC. It dissects the statutory payment priority stack during liquidation, the absolute supremacy of the CoC's economic decisions, and the forensic mapping of fraudulent transactions.

core_concepts.title: The Liquidation Waterfall Mechanism (Section 53)
core_concepts.description:
If a company fails to resolve and enters liquidation, its assets are sold and distributed strictly according to the statutory 'Waterfall' hierarchy. One layer must be paid 100% before the next layer receives a single rupee:
1. CIRP and Liquidation process costs (paid first in full).
2. Workmen's dues (for the preceding 24 months) AND Secured Creditors who waived their security interest (Ranked completely equal/pari passu).
3. Wages and unpaid dues to employees (preceding 12 months).
4. Unsecured Financial Creditors.
5. Central and State Government dues (preceding 24 months) AND Unsecured debts of secured creditors.
6. Preference Shareholders.
7. Equity Shareholders (Paid last).

core_concepts.title: The Inviolability of the 'Commercial Wisdom' of the CoC
core_concepts.description:
A foundational constitutional jurisprudence established by the Supreme Court in *K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank* and solidified in the *Essar Steel (2019)* case.
- The Rule: The NCLT and NCLAT have **ZERO jurisdiction to review the business or commercial decisions** of the CoC. If the CoC, by a 66% majority, rejects or approves a resolution plan based on its economic feasibility, the NCLT cannot sit in appeal over it. Judicial review is strictly limited to verifying if the plan violates any parameters of Section 30(2) (such as paying liquidation value to operational creditors).

core_concepts.title: PUFE Transactions (Avoidance / Forensic Audits)
core_concepts.description:
The Resolution Professional is legally mandated to conduct forensic reviews to claw back assets illegally transferred by promoters before bankruptcy. These are categorized as **PUFE** transactions:
- **P**referential [Sec 43]: Giving an unfair advantage to one creditor over others within a 'look-back period' of 1 year (or 2 years for related parties).
- **U**ndervalued [Sec 45]: Transferring assets for a consideration significantly less than the actual market value within the look-back window.
- **F**raudulent/Wrongful Trading [Sec 66]: Carrying on business with the explicit intent to defraud creditors. Promoters can be held *personally liable* without any limit.
- **E**xtortionate Credit [Sec 50]: Entering unconscionable credit terms that exploit the debtor within the preceding 2 years.

core_concepts.title: Section 29A: The Promoter Bar
core_concepts.description:
The moral conscience of the Code, inserted to prevent structural moral hazard.
- The Rule: It absolutely bars certain persons from submitting a resolution plan to buy back their own company. Most notably, **wilful defaulters, disqualified directors, or promoters of a corporate debtor that has been an NPA for 1+ years** are disqualified. Promoters cannot intentionally bankrupt their company to wipe out debts and buy it back at a discount.

important_entities.name: Equality vs. Equity in Distribution (*Essar Steel Rule*)
important_entities.key_fact: Operational creditors do not have an automatic right to equal pay with financial creditors.
important_entities.significance: The Supreme Court ruled that 'equality' under the IBC means equitable treatment *within the same class of creditors*, not across different classes. Financial creditors take the ultimate commercial risk and are secured, hence they can legally be paid higher percentages than operational creditors in a resolution plan, as long as operational creditors get at least their hypothetical liquidation value.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams constantly test this statutory exception. Under **Section 240A**, the stringent disqualification of promoters under Section 29A (clauses c and h) **does NOT apply to MSMEs**. The promoters of an MSME *are* legally permitted to submit a resolution plan for their own company, provided they are not wilful defaulters or otherwise personally disqualified, recognizing that outside buyers are rarely found for small local businesses.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Memorize the PUFE acronym to systematically tackle corporate fraud asset-clawback questions.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Law Optional or Judiciary Mains, when evaluating the success of the IBC, you must structurally analyze the **Section 53 Waterfall** hierarchy and link it with the economic theory of the 'Ease of Doing Business' and unlocking non-performing assets (NPAs).
